context.concept_name: Matching chart type to the specific point being made (trend vs. comparison vs. distribution vs. part-to-whole)

coverage.learning_objective: Match a chart type to the specific point being communicated to a stakeholder audience (trend, comparison, distribution, or part-to-whole), distinct from choosing a chart type for one's own exploration.

required_facts.statement: A bar chart is used for graphing categorical data and comparing values across categories.
Line graphs are best when you want to show how the value of something changes over time, or compare how several things change over time relative to each other.
Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side.

A pie chart expresses a part-to-whole relationship in the data, and is best used either for a general sense of how parts relate to the whole, or to highlight that one segment is notably larger or smaller than the others; the pie must depict a meaningful whole (values that sum to 100%).

A boxplot may be unfamiliar to many people and could introduce a learning curve; choosing a different display altogether may avoid confusion for audiences who do not know this chart type or how to read it.
source_refs: swd_what_is_a_boxplot#When should you not use a boxplot?

required_facts.statement: A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it, though it can still be designed to convey findings to an audience.

misconceptions.statement: It is just as easy to precisely compare the sizes of pie slices as it is to compare bar lengths.

teaching_blocks.content: During your own exploration, you might have built a bar chart, a line plot, and a box plot of the delivery data. Presenting to the operations manager, the question changes: which one actually makes the Lagos point, for this audience?

A bar chart is used for graphing categorical data and comparing values across categories -- showing average delivery time side by side across Lagos, Abuja, and Kano. Line graphs are best when you want to show how the value of something changes over time, or compare how several things change over time relative to each other -- showing Lagos delivery time rising week over week. Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side -- but a boxplot may be unfamiliar to many people and could introduce a learning curve, so choosing a different display altogether may avoid confusion for audiences who do not know this chart type or how to read it; for a manager who hasn't seen a box plot before, the bar chart or line plot can often make the point more directly.

A pie chart expresses a part-to-whole relationship in the data, and is best used either for a general sense of how parts relate to the whole, or to highlight that one segment is notably larger or smaller than the others; the pie must depict a meaningful whole (values that sum to 100%). If the point is "Lagos accounts for most of our total delivery volume," a pie chart of each city's share of total orders fits that part-to-whole framing in a way a bar chart of averages would not.

A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it, though it can still be designed to convey findings to an audience -- useful to keep in mind if the distance/delivery-time relationship ever needs to go in front of the manager directly, rather than staying an exploratory chart.

It can look like comparing pie slices is just as easy as comparing bar lengths, since both show a value at a glance -- but it is not. A bar chart's aligned, common baseline makes length differences easy to judge; two pie slices of similar size are harder to rank correctly by eye.

video_need.reason: Choosing which chart best makes a specific point is clearest when the same delivery data is shown rendered as a bar chart, a line plot, and a pie chart side by side, so the audience can see directly why one framing lands and another doesn't -- a side-by-side visual the text's description can only approximate.

media.group_title: Why the chart type must match the point you are making

segments.label: Bar chart vs. pie chart: comparing values across categories
segments.summary: The same time-use data (sleep, work, eat, rest) is shown first as a pie chart, then as a bar chart. The pie makes it hard to judge which slice is larger when two slices are close in size. The bar chart, with its common baseline, makes the one-hour difference between working and sleeping immediately readable. A second example pits two pie charts against a grouped bar chart to answer 'does Earl work more than Herman, and by how much?' — a question the pies struggle to answer and the bar chart resolves at a glance.

segments.label: Boxplots: strong for distributions, but risky with unfamiliar audiences
segments.summary: A boxplot is considered as a candidate for showing distributions across multiple groups. Two practical problems emerge: sparse data on some days would produce boxes with no box body, and — more broadly — boxplots are not a widely recognised chart type, so an audience unfamiliar with them faces a steeper learning curve. The presenter notes that a specialist audience (researchers and physicians) may be the exception, but still sets the boxplot aside in favour of continuing to explore other options.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the same data looks different depending on chart type, and notice when a chart makes comparison easy versus hard. The first clip argues strongly for bars over pies; Devspace's text also covers when a pie is the right choice.
bridge_note.after: The first clip demonstrates f1 and counters the pie-slice comparison misconception; the second covers f3 and f5. Neither clip addresses part-to-whole framing (f4) or scatterplots (f6) — the text covers both.

practice_anchor.objective: Given the stakeholder point 'this category dominates the total', choose one chart type from the set {bar chart, line graph, boxplot, pie chart, scatterplot} and write one sentence justifying why it best communicates that specific point to a non-technical audience.
practice_anchor.success: The learner selects the pie chart (or provides a well-reasoned case for a bar chart showing share), correctly invokes the part-to-whole requirement (values sum to 100%), and explains why the chosen type makes the dominance of one segment immediately visible to a non-technical reader.

visual_anchor.purpose: A side-by-side display of the same delivery-volume data rendered as a bar chart (city vs. city comparison), a pie chart (each city's share of total orders), and a line plot (Lagos delivery time over weeks), with the stakeholder point each chart is suited to labelled beneath it — making visible why chart choice is driven by the point, not by the data alone.

teaching_notes: TOC conflict: f4 requires teaching what a pie chart is and when it fits, but no viz concept in this path teaches matplotlib pie-chart creation syntax. Teach the pie chart as a communication-design concept only (what it shows, when it fits, its part-to-whole requirement) -- no plt.pie() code is given here, since no earlier concept taught it.

context.concept_name: Simplifying a technical chart for a non-technical audience (removing gridlines, axis clutter, unneeded precision)

coverage.learning_objective: Simplify a technical-looking chart for a non-technical audience by removing gridlines, chart borders, and unneeded label precision, without changing the underlying data.

required_facts.statement: Gridlines can be deleted from a chart; if precise values matter to the audience, label the data point(s) directly instead of relying on gridlines.
A chart's border can be removed, since it is not adding informative value; white space can differentiate parts of a visual better than a border.
Data labels should be used sparingly, only where the exact values are important to the audience; otherwise they should be removed and the axis used instead.
Reducing clutter lets the audience use their attention to decide what actions might be warranted, rather than working out how to read the graph.
Unnecessary trailing zeroes can be dropped from axis labels.
Diagonally rotated axis text is slower to read; labels can be abbreviated so they render horizontally instead.

teaching_blocks.content: A bar chart of city delivery times built during your own exploration can carry gridlines, a border, and precise decimal labels that help you double-check the numbers. The operations manager probably doesn't need any of that to get the point.

Gridlines can be deleted from a chart; if precise values matter to the audience, label the data point(s) directly instead of relying on gridlines. A chart's border can be removed, since it is not adding informative value; white space can differentiate parts of a visual better than a border.

Data labels should be used sparingly, only where the exact values are important to the audience; otherwise they should be removed and the axis used instead. Unnecessary trailing zeroes can be dropped from axis labels, and diagonally rotated axis text is slower to read, so labels can be abbreviated so they render horizontally instead -- "22.00 minutes" can become "22 min", and city-name tick labels don't need to be rotated at all when the names are as short as Lagos, Abuja, and Kano.

Reducing clutter lets the audience use their attention to decide what actions might be warranted, rather than working out how to read the graph -- none of these changes alter the underlying delivery-time numbers, only how much visual effort it takes to read them.

video_need.reason: Decluttering is inherently a before/after transformation of the same chart -- gridlines, a border, and rotated labels present, then removed -- which is far more persuasive watched applied to one chart than read as a list of removals.

media.group_title: Decluttering a chart for a non-technical audience

segments.label: Removing chart clutter: border, gridlines, trailing zeros, diagonal labels, and excess data labels
segments.summary: The presenter opens by explaining that every chart element adds cognitive burden, and that overwhelming an audience risks losing them entirely — establishing why decluttering matters. Working on a bar chart in Excel, they remove the chart border (noting white space does the job of separation better), delete the gridlines and shaded background, then reformat the y-axis to drop trailing zeros by switching to thousands units with a 'k' suffix. They then abbreviate the diagonal month labels on the x-axis to horizontal text, citing research that diagonal text takes fifty percent longer to read. Finally, they weigh whether exact values are needed: deciding they are not, they delete all data labels and keep the y-axis instead, leaving a much cleaner chart.

bridge_note.before: Watch how each removal reduces reading effort. Note: the presenter uses Excel; the same design principles apply in any charting tool. The clip does not demonstrate labelling a data point directly when precision matters (f1).
bridge_note.after: The clip shows f2–f6 applied in sequence. Devspace's text also covers f1: when precise values are essential, label the data point directly rather than restoring gridlines.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a bar chart that has a visible border, gridlines, trailing-zero axis labels (e.g. '22.00'), diagonally rotated city-name tick labels, and data labels on every bar, simplify it for a non-technical operations manager: remove the border and gridlines, drop the trailing zeros from axis labels, abbreviate and horizontalise the city-name tick labels, and remove the data labels (keeping the axis for approximate reading).
practice_anchor.success: The revised chart has no border, no gridlines, axis labels without trailing zeros, horizontal (non-rotated) city-name tick labels, and no per-bar data labels — while the underlying delivery-time values are unchanged.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the same bar chart twice side by side: the 'before' version with a border, gridlines, decimal axis labels, rotated city-name tick labels, and data labels on every bar; the 'after' version with all of those removed, illustrating how each removal reduces visual effort without changing the data.

teaching_notes: No specific matplotlib method names are given by the facts for removing gridlines/borders (e.g. no ax.grid(False) is stated), so the example stays at the conceptual/design level rather than inventing exact syntax.

clusters.title: Matching and Simplifying Charts for an Audience
clusters.reasoning: Choosing the right chart type for the point being made and simplifying charts for a non-technical audience are two aspects of the same skill: making a visualization communicate clearly. They read as two parts of one idea: chart design for stakeholder communication.
